name: Pentapeptide-18

angle.text: Sold as Leuphasyl, this enkephalin-mimic is promoted as a 'Botox-like' ingredient to soften expression lines. Human evidence comes from a retinol combination cream, so its separate contribution is untested.

summary: An enkephalin-mimic peptide sold for expression lines; the human evidence is a retinol combination cream.
note: Wrinkle data come from a combination cream with retinol, not the peptide alone.
currentQuick:
Pentapeptide-18 is a short peptide marketed as Leuphasyl for fine expression lines, often described as a topical, 'Botox-like' ingredient.
Published work is mostly formulation and cell studies; the one human study used a cream that also contained retinol.
How it works: It is described as an enkephalin mimic that binds receptors at nerve endings, closing calcium channels and reducing acetylcholine release, though the cited papers did not directly test this in skin.
Risks and caveats: No peptide-specific adverse events were found in the sources; retinol in the studied cream was linked to extra peeling. It is a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Pentapeptide-18 (Tyr-D-Ala-Gly-Phe-Leu), sold by supplier Lipotec as Leuphasyl, is a cosmetic peptide marketed to soften expression lines. Papers describe it as an enkephalin mimic that is proposed to bind enkephalin receptors on nerve endings, close calcium channels and reduce acetylcholine release, a mechanism sometimes called 'Botox-like' .
Published evidence on the peptide alone is sparse. A 2024 study of a retinol-and-pentapeptide-18 eye cream reported wrinkle-area reductions in 20 women, but the cream's effect cannot be separated from retinol . Research on the peptide itself consists largely of formulation and in vitro work .

name: Pentapeptide-3

angle.text: The name is ambiguous: formerly the KTTKS collagen peptide (Matrixyl), and linked to Vialox, a 'Botox-like' ingredient. Users take it for smoother, less lined skin; verified evidence for either use is scarce.

summary: An ambiguous peptide name: historically KTTKS (Matrixyl), also tied to Vialox; little verified evidence.
note: The name referred to different peptides at different times; check the full ingredient name.
currentQuick:
Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide label whose meaning has changed: before 2006 it denoted palmitoyl KTTKS (Matrixyl), and it is also tied to the Vialox brand.
Research is mostly laboratory work on KTTKS-type peptides, and no clinical trial specific to Vialox was found.
How it works: KTTKS-type peptides are described as matrikines that signal cells to make collagen and other matrix proteins; Vialox is described by suppliers as reducing muscle signalling, which this wiki could not verify.
Risks and caveats: No adverse events were reported in the sources. A cell study found KTTKS analogues non-cytotoxic to fibroblasts.
deepLead:
Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide name that is ambiguous in the literature. Before 2006, the INCI name palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 referred to the Lys-Thr-Thr-Lys-Ser (KTTKS) peptide sold as Matrixyl, since renamed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 . the available alias for this entry, Vialox, is separately marketed as a muscle-relaxing 'Botox-like' ingredient, and no loaded source describes it.
Available research on the KTTKS peptide family shows effects on collagen and extracellular-matrix production in cultured cells, and a 2019 study of 32 KTTKS analogues found none cytotoxic to fibroblasts . No clinical study of a product specified as Vialox was found.

name: Oligopeptide-68

angle.text: Skin-brightening serum users take this peptide to fade dark spots and melasma and even out tone. Human data are small melasma studies of multi-ingredient products.

summary: A cosmetic peptide marketed as a tyrosinase inhibitor for brightening; human data are limited to small melasma studies of multi-ingredient products.
note: Studied only in combination formulas, so its individual contribution is not isolated.
currentQuick:
Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide described in the literature as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic that inhibits the enzyme tyrosinase, which is involved in making melanin. It is sold as a skin-brightening ingredient in serums and creams.
The available human research consists of two melasma studies in which it was one component of a multi-ingredient regimen, so what it does on its own has not been separated out.
How it works: According to the study authors, oligopeptide-68 inhibits tyrosinase activity, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis [1]. In one study it was paired with diacetyl boldine, which is described as stabilizing tyrosinase in its inactive form [1].
Risks and caveats: The studies reviewed here were of combination products that also contained exfoliating acids, sunscreen filters or other depigmenting agents, so adverse effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone. It is a cosmetic ingredient in the US and EU rather than a drug.
deepLead:
Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide that is marketed as a skin-brightening ingredient. In the dermatology literature it is described as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic oligopeptide that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production .
Interest in looksmaxxing and skincare communities centres on its use against uneven pigmentation and melasma. The published human evidence is limited to two studies of multi-ingredient melasma regimens in which oligopeptide-68 was one component .

name: Tetrapeptide-21

angle.text: This GEKG peptide appears in anti-aging skincare for collagen support and firmer-looking skin. Research so far covers skin delivery and cell-culture effects rather than human trials.

summary: A four-amino-acid (GEKG) matrix-supporting cosmetic peptide; research so far is on skin delivery and cell-culture effects, not human trials.
note: No published human efficacy trial in the available literature.
currentQuick:
Tetrapeptide-21 is a short cosmetic peptide with the amino acid sequence GEKG, sold in anti-aging serums as a matrix-supporting ingredient. Papers describe it as having collagen-stimulating, anti-aging activity.
Most published work concerns how to get it through the skin, with a 2018 delivery study and a 2026 hydrogel study, plus an in vitro fibroblast study. No human clinical trial of its appearance effects was found.
How it works: It is described as stimulating collagen and the extracellular matrix [2]. Because peptides are large, polar and easily degraded, researchers have studied enhancer molecules, carrier systems and elastin-derived hydrogels to improve skin delivery [1][2].
Risks and caveats: No safety data from human trials were found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug.
deepLead:
Tetrapeptide-21 is a cosmetic peptide with the sequence GEKG that is used in anti-aging skincare. Published papers describe it as demonstrating anti-aging efficacy and stimulating collagen .
The literature on it is mostly formulation science: peptides are hard to deliver into skin because of their size, hydrophilicity, polarity and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation . No human clinical trial of its effect on appearance was found.

name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-3

angle.text: Used in topical products for thinning hair, usually within the Capixyl blend with biochanin A and ginseng, to look for thicker, fuller hair. It was tested only inside a multi-herbal combination against 3% minoxidil in one small trial.

summary: A hair-anchoring cosmetic peptide (found in Capixyl) tested only inside a multi-herbal combination against 3% minoxidil in one small trial.
note: The only listed trial tested a combination product, in 32 people.
currentQuick:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide used in hair-density topicals and is named as the hair-anchoring ingredient in Capixyl. It is usually combined with plant extracts.
One 24-week randomized, triple-blind trial in 32 people compared a combination of biochanin A, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 and ginseng extracts with 3% minoxidil solution in androgenetic alopecia, so the peptide's own effect was not isolated.
How it works: Mechanistic claims are made by product makers; the studies reviewed here evaluated outcomes of the combination rather than the peptide's mechanism.
Risks and caveats: The trial assessed a safety profile for the combination as a stated objective [1]. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than an approved hair-loss drug.
deepLead:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide used in topical hair products for thinning hair, commonly as part of the ingredient blend Capixyl, which also appears with biochanin A and ginseng extracts .
A 24-week randomized, triple-blind controlled trial in 32 men and women with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia compared a combination of biochanin A, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 and ginseng extracts with 3% minoxidil solution . A 2026 systematic review examined peptides for hair loss in clinical trials .

name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3

angle.text: Appears in serum ingredient lists as a signal peptide, where users expect smoother, firmer-looking skin. It is found in patent compositions with plant extracts; no published human trials exist for it.

summary: A cosmetic signal peptide that shows up in serum ingredient lists, with no published human trials behind it.
note: Known only as one ingredient in multi-ingredient formulations; no clinical studies found.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a short peptide linked to a fatty chain, used as an ingredient in some skin-care products. It is grouped with other cosmetic signal peptides.
It is documented mainly in patent filings that list it among many ingredients. No human trials of the ingredient itself were found.
How it works: Signal peptides are generally described by manufacturers as messengers that prompt skin cells; the sources reviewed here do not describe a tested mechanism for this specific peptide.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to this ingredient were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient rather than as an approved drug.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic ingredient classed among the signal peptides, short amino-acid chains attached to a fatty (palmitoyl) group and added to skin-care products. It appears by name in the ingredient lists of published patent compositions for topical products, where it is combined with plant extracts and other actives .
Published scientific literature on this specific ingredient is sparse in the sources reviewed for this wiki. No clinical trial of palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 was found, and the available records only show it as one listed component of multi-ingredient formulations, so its effect on appearance has not been established by independent human studies.

name: Deoxyarbutin

angle.text: Used as a topical lightener to fade age spots, melasma and other dark patches for a more even tone. Evidence comes mostly from lab and animal work, with thin human trial data.

summary: A synthetic arbutin derivative that blocks tyrosinase in lab and animal work; human trial data are thin.
note: Evidence is mostly in vitro and animal; one study examined UVB-irradiated deoxyarbutin cytotoxicity.
currentQuick:
Deoxyarbutin is a lab-made relative of arbutin studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven pigment.
It was reported in 2005 to lighten skin in guinea pigs and to inhibit tyrosinase more potently than hydroquinone in a test-tube assay. Published human trials were not found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It competes with tyrosine at tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, reducing melanin production; studies describe the inhibition as reversible.
Risks and caveats: Researchers have compared its safety with hydroquinone in cultured cells and examined cytotoxicity of UVB-irradiated forms. Regulatory status was not established in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Deoxyarbutin (dA) is a synthetic derivative of arbutin that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and has been developed as a topical skin-lightening agent for hyperpigmentation such as age spots and melasma .
It was described in a 2005 paper as a reversible tyrosinase inhibitor with skin-lightening activity in a pigmented guinea pig model and with inhibition of mushroom tyrosinase more potent than hydroquinone or arbutin in vitro . Later laboratory work has examined its safety relative to hydroquinone, and its stability in formulations . The sources reviewed contain no randomized human trial results for deoxyarbutin as a cosmetic.

name: Aloesin

angle.text: This Aloe-derived compound is studied as a topical lightener for dark spots and uneven tone. Evidence for that use is lab-level, and no published trials were found.

summary: An Aloe-derived tyrosinase inhibitor with lab-level evidence for lightening and no published trials found.
note: Evidence is enzyme, cell and UV-induced pigmentation work; no controlled trials found.
currentQuick:
Aloesin is a compound from the Aloe plant studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots.
Research is mostly in test tubes, cells and a 2002 report on UV-induced pigmentation; controlled trials in people were not found.
How it works: It competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to act synergistically with arbutin.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no human safety data specific to topical aloesin; most reports concern laboratory and animal models.
deepLead:
Aloesin is a chromone glucoside isolated from the Aloe plant that has been studied as a topical skin-lightening agent because it inhibits tyrosinase, the key enzyme of melanin synthesis . It is also among the best-studied active constituents of Aloe vera alongside aloe-emodin, aloin, emodin and acemannan .
Laboratory studies reported that aloesin competitively inhibits tyrosinase and reduces melanin production in vitro, and a 2002 study reported that it inhibited UV-induced hyperpigmentation . Reviews of botanical skin-lightening agents discuss it alongside other plant extracts . The sources reviewed contain no randomized clinical trial results for aloesin.

name: Ellagic acid

angle.text: This fruit and nut polyphenol appears in some skin-care products as a brightener, and users take it as an antioxidant. No skin trials were found for the brightening use.

summary: A fruit-and-nut polyphenol sold as an antioxidant and brightener; no skin trials found.
note: Poor absorption; supplement health claims have drawn FDA warning letters.
currentQuick:
Ellagic acid is a polyphenol found in pomegranates, berries and walnuts, used in supplements and some skin-care products as an antioxidant or brightener.
Research is mostly laboratory-based; no trial of its brightening effect on skin was found.
How it works: It scavenges free radicals in laboratory assays and is converted by gut bacteria into urolithins, which are better absorbed than the parent compound.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports the FDA has warned supplement companies over disease claims. No safety profile was found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Ellagic acid is a naturally occurring polyphenol, the dilactone of hexahydroxydiphenic acid, found in foods such as pomegranates, raspberries, strawberries, walnuts and grapes, where it is released from ellagitannins . It is marketed as an antioxidant and, in some skin-care products, as a brightening ingredient.
Most research concerns its antioxidant activity and its gut-microbiota metabolites, the urolithins . The sources reviewed contain no clinical trial of ellagic acid for skin brightening. Wikipedia reports that it is sold as a supplement with claims against cancer and other diseases, that there is no scientific evidence for such claims, and that the FDA has issued warning letters over such claims .

name: 4-n-Butylresorcinol

angle.text: Used in serums and creams for melasma and age spots to even out tone. Several small randomized trials have reported improvement for this use.

summary: A tyrosinase inhibitor used in melasma and dark-spot serums, with several small randomized trials reporting improvement.
note: Trials are small and short; head-to-head comparisons are limited.
currentQuick:
4-n-Butylresorcinol is a lab-made ingredient found in serums for melasma and dark spots.
Several small randomized trials, including split-face and vehicle-controlled designs, have reported pigment improvement, though sample sizes are modest.
How it works: It inhibits tyrosinase and has been reported to affect tyrosinase-related protein-1, reducing melanin production in cells.
Risks and caveats: Reports in the sources describe minimal irritation at studied concentrations; regulation varies by country, and figures from secondary summaries should be verified.
deepLead:
4-n-Butylresorcinol (also called butylresorcinol or rucinol) is a synthetic resorcinol derivative used in topical serums and creams aimed at hyperpigmentation such as melasma and age spots. It acts as a tyrosinase inhibitor .
Unlike many other tyrosinase inhibitors, it has been tested in several small randomized human trials in melasma and other pigmentation, with reported improvements versus vehicle . These trials are small and short, and independent comparisons with other agents are limited.

name: Rhododendrol

angle.text: Developed as a skin-lightening cosmetic ingredient to brighten tone, it was used until July 2013, when it was withdrawn after reports of patchy depigmentation. It is documented here as a historical product.

summary: A cosmetic lightening agent withdrawn in 2013 after users developed patchy depigmentation (leukoderma).
note: Withdrawn after leukoderma reports; documented melanocyte toxicity via tyrosinase.
currentQuick:
Rhododendrol was a plant-derived whitening ingredient in Japanese cosmetics. Reports of patchy white skin among users led to its withdrawal in 2013.
It now appears in research as an example of how a tyrosinase inhibitor can damage the pigment cells it acts on.
How it works: It inhibits tyrosinase but is also oxidized by the enzyme into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes; immune responses have also been studied.
Risks and caveats: Documented harm is leukoderma. Wikipedia reports that pigment returns in most cases after stopping, and that its use has been prohibited since 2013.
deepLead:
Rhododendrol (RD, related to raspberry ketone) is a phenolic compound that occurs naturally in Rhododendron and other plants and was developed as a melanin-synthesis inhibitor for skin-lightening cosmetics . It was used as a skin-whitening agent until July 2013, when reports emerged that users had developed patchy depigmentation (leukoderma), after which the products were withdrawn .
Subsequent research examined why a tyrosinase inhibitor produced depigmentation. Studies found that tyrosinase oxidizes rhododendrol into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes, and some work has also examined immune involvement . It is mainly discussed today as a case study in cosmetic depigmenting-agent safety.

name: Monobenzone

angle.text: A prescription depigmenting cream used for extensive vitiligo so remaining skin matches the pale patches. Forums discuss it as a permanent route to lighter skin, though that use outside vitiligo is off-label and the effect is described as irreversible.

summary: A prescription depigmenting cream for extensive vitiligo whose skin-whitening effect is permanent, which is why forums discuss it as a one-way option.
note: Depigmentation is described as irreversible; approved only for extensive vitiligo, and no trials exist for cosmetic lightening of normal skin.
currentQuick:
Monobenzone is a topical drug that permanently removes pigment from skin. Its approved use is in people with widespread vitiligo, where it evens out the remaining normal skin to match the depigmented patches.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a permanent skin whitener, with members debating whether to go paler than their natural tone. No trial has tested it for that purpose.
How it works: Tyrosinase in melanocytes converts monobenzone into reactive quinones that bind to cellular proteins. Laboratory studies report that this triggers an immune response against pigmented cells, leading to lasting loss of melanocytes.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include irritation, contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and depigmentation at untreated sites. The effect is described as permanent and does not reverse after stopping. It is prescription-only in the US; online gray-market purchasing is discussed in forums.
deepLead:
Monobenzone, also called monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH) or 4-(benzyloxy)phenol, is a topical depigmenting agent. In the United States it is a prescription-only drug used to permanently remove remaining skin pigment in people with extensive vitiligo, so that the unaffected skin matches the depigmented patches . Unlike milder skin-lightening ingredients, its effect is described in the literature as irreversible, because it leads to the loss of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells .
Laboratory research has found that monobenzone is converted by tyrosinase inside melanocytes into reactive quinone species that bind to proteins and make pigmented cells a target for the immune system, rather than only blocking pigment production . That immune mechanism has also been investigated in melanoma, in a small phase 2a trial combining monobenzone with imiquimod .
In looksmaxxing communities, monobenzone is discussed as a 'permanent skin whitener' and as a product that some members consider using to lighten their overall skin tone, with ordering from online pharmacies and gray-market sellers described in forum threads . No published trial has evaluated it as a cosmetic lightener in people without vitiligo, and its depigmentation is not reversible once established .

name: Oxyresveratrol

angle.text: This mulberry-derived stilbene is discussed as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven tone. Its tyrosinase inhibition is shown in the lab; no human skin trials back the brightening claims.

summary: A mulberry-derived stilbene that strongly blocks tyrosinase in the lab, with no human skin trials behind the brightening claims.
note: Evidence is test-tube and animal only; light sensitive.
currentQuick:
Oxyresveratrol is a natural compound from mulberry and related plants. It is a strong tyrosinase inhibitor in laboratory tests, which is why it is mentioned as a skin-brightening ingredient.
I found no human trials of it for pigmentation or skin appearance.
How it works: Tyrosinase is the enzyme that drives melanin production. Laboratory studies on mushroom and mouse melanoma tyrosinase report potent inhibition by oxyresveratrol.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data for skin use were found. It is reported to be light sensitive and to degrade under UV exposure.
deepLead:
Oxyresveratrol (2,3',4,5'-tetrahydroxystilbene) is a plant-derived stilbenoid found in species of Morus (mulberry) and Artocarpus, among others . It is studied mainly for its strong inhibition of tyrosinase, the enzyme that carries out rate-limiting steps of melanin synthesis, and is therefore discussed as a potential skin-lightening ingredient .
The evidence for this comes from test-tube and cell work, mostly using mushroom tyrosinase and mouse melanoma cell enzymes . Other laboratory and animal studies have reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects . No human trials of oxyresveratrol for skin appearance were found.

name: Resveratrol topical

angle.text: Used in anti-aging and brightening serums as an antioxidant for a fresher, more even look. Evidence includes one small recent trial, with most research focused on delivery formulations.

summary: An antioxidant stilbene sold in anti-aging serums, with one small recent trial and mostly delivery-formulation research behind it.
note: Poorly stable and poorly absorbed; human skin evidence is a few small studies.
currentQuick:
Topical resveratrol is a plant antioxidant used in anti-aging and brightening skincare. Research so far has centered on how to get it into skin and keep it stable.
One 8-week randomized trial in women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of aging, but the human evidence base is small.
How it works: It is marketed as an antioxidant. Studies on delivery show nanocarriers and emulsions can raise how much stays in the skin in laboratory models.
Risks and caveats: The sources describe no topical adverse-effect data; reported side effects of resveratrol are mainly gastrointestinal with high oral intake. It is light sensitive and degrades easily.
deepLead:
Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a plant polyphenol found in grape skins, berries and peanuts, and in knotweed root used for supplements . Applied to the skin, it appears in anti-aging and brightening cosmetics, where it is marketed as an antioxidant .
Much of the published topical work concerns delivery: resveratrol has low water solubility and is photosensitive, and researchers have tested nanocarriers, emulsions and gels to improve skin retention . Human evidence on appearance is sparse. An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy women over 40 reported reduced visible signs of skin aging with trans-resveratrol , and small registered trials of resveratrol-containing products exist . Wikipedia's general resveratrol article states that there is no significant evidence of an effect on aging skin .

name: Licochalcone A

angle.text: This licorice-root compound appears in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin and is also discussed for possible brightening via pigment reduction. Lab work hints at tyrosinase inhibition, and human trials are combination-product acne studies.

summary: A licorice-root chalcone used in soothing skincare, with lab hints of tyrosinase inhibition and only combination-product acne trials in humans.
note: Human data are multi-ingredient acne products; pigment and redness claims rest on lab work.
currentQuick:
Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root that shows up in sensitive-skin and acne-care products. It is also discussed for possible brightening effects.
Human studies found were acne trials of moisturizers containing several actives, so its own effect cannot be isolated.
How it works: Laboratory work reports antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no skin safety data. Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, relevant to handling rather than finished products.
deepLead:
Licochalcone A is a chalcone-type phenol isolated from the roots of licorice species (Glycyrrhiza inflata and G. glabra) . In skincare it appears in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin and is also discussed for its possible effect on pigment production .
Laboratory research has reported antioxidant, antibacterial, antimalarial and anticancer activity , and licorice flavonoids have been examined for tyrosinase inhibition . Human data on appearance come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so the contribution of licochalcone A alone cannot be separated .

name: Chitosan

angle.text: Sold as a fat-binding supplement for weight loss, and used as a carrier in cosmetics. No trial shows a skin-pigment or appearance effect from it.

summary: A shellfish-derived polysaccharide used as a carrier in cosmetics and sold as a fat binder, with no trial showing a skin-pigment or appearance effect.
note: Crustacean-derived forms may carry allergenic proteins; weight-loss reviews report no significant effect.
currentQuick:
Chitosan is a natural polymer made from chitin in shellfish shells. For appearance it mainly shows up as a delivery carrier in skincare formulations and as a weight-loss supplement.
I found no human studies of chitosan for skin pigmentation. Reviews cited by Wikipedia report no significant weight or cholesterol effect from supplements.
How it works: Its amine groups become positively charged in acid, letting it form films, gels and nanoparticles that stick to tissue and carry other ingredients.
Risks and caveats: Crustacean-derived chitosan may carry allergenic proteins, according to Grokipedia. The FDA warned in 2015 about exaggerated weight-loss claims.
deepLead:
Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide made by partially deacetylating chitin, which is found mainly in the shells of shrimp and crabs and in some fungi and insects . It dissolves in dilute acid and is widely used in medicine, agriculture and industry, with cosmetic uses and weight-loss supplements being the applications most relevant to appearance .
In appearance contexts it appears in two main forms: as a carrier polymer in topical and nanoparticle formulations, for example to improve skin retention of actives such as resveratrol, and as an over-the-counter 'fat binder' supplement. Wikipedia reports that reviews in 2008 and 2016 found no significant effect of chitosan on weight or cholesterol, and that the US FDA issued a 2015 advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers . Sources reviewed contain no controlled evidence that chitosan inhibits skin pigmentation in people.

name: Diacetyl boldine

angle.text: Found in serums for hyperpigmentation, dark spots and melasma, usually as one part of a multi-ingredient formula. Evidence is small combination-formula studies, with no stand-alone trials.

summary: A boldo-derived tyrosinase-stabilizing brightener found in serums, with small combination-formula studies and no stand-alone trials.
note: Published human data come from multi-ingredient formulas, so DAB's own effect is not isolated.
currentQuick:
Diacetyl boldine is an ingredient made from boldine, an alkaloid from the boldo tree. It appears in brightening serums aimed at dark spots and melasma.
Published human studies are few and test it inside multi-ingredient products, some compared against hydroquinone. Whether it works on its own has not been tested separately.
How it works: A melasma study describes it as stabilizing tyrosinase, the enzyme that produces melanin, in its inactive form.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed report no specific adverse-event data for the ingredient. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, and trial registrations for serums that may contain it list no posted results.
deepLead:
Diacetyl boldine (DAB) is a cosmetic skin-brightening ingredient derived from boldine, an aporphine alkaloid found in the bark of the boldo tree (Peumus boldus) . It is used in serums and creams aimed at hyperpigmentation, dark spots and melasma, usually as one component of a multi-ingredient formula.
According to a published melasma study, DAB acts by stabilizing tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, in its inactive form . Published human evidence is limited to a small number of formulation studies in which DAB was combined with other agents, so its effect on its own has not been isolated .

name: Mulberry extract

angle.text: Marketed in skincare as a botanical brightener for a more even tone. Published research concerns blood sugar and antioxidants, not skin tone.

summary: A botanical 'brightener' whose published research is about blood sugar and antioxidants, not skin tone.
note: No human skin-brightening trial was found in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Mulberry extract comes from Morus trees and is sold in skincare as a plant brightener, with mulberroside F named as the active compound.
The studies found concern other uses, mainly blood glucose and antioxidant chemistry. No human trial of it for skin tone turned up.
How it works: Cosmetic marketing attributes brightening to mulberroside F. The sources reviewed do not document a mechanism in human skin.
Risks and caveats: No skin-specific safety data were found. Mulberry fruit and leaf are common food and supplement ingredients.
deepLead:
Mulberry extract is a plant extract from trees of the genus Morus, marketed in skincare as a botanical brightener, with mulberroside F named as its skin-lightening constituent. The fruit and leaves are also sold as dietary supplements .
The material reviewed here contains no human study of topical mulberry extract for skin tone. Published mulberry research concerns other uses: blood-glucose effects, antioxidant chemistry and food science.

name: Rice bran extract

angle.text: Popular in K-beauty and J-beauty products for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects. Evidence includes antioxidant and cell-culture data, with no controlled human skin-tone trial found.

summary: A K-beauty brightening botanical with antioxidant and cell-culture data but no controlled human skin-tone trial found.
note: Human efficacy claims come largely from an AI-generated encyclopedia summary and lab studies.
currentQuick:
Rice bran extract comes from the outer layer of milled rice and appears in Asian skincare for brightening and hydration. Rice bran and rice water have a long history of traditional use.
Lab studies show antioxidant activity, and a fermented extract reduced melanin-pathway signaling in mouse cells. Controlled human trials for skin tone were not found.
How it works: Constituents such as ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol and tocopherols act as antioxidants in test systems, and in melanoma cells a fermented extract lowered MITF, a regulator of melanin production.
Risks and caveats: Safety assessments summarized by Grokipedia describe low irritation potential at typical cosmetic concentrations; that summary was not independently verified.
deepLead:
Rice bran extract is a cosmetic ingredient derived from the bran layer of rice (Oryza sativa), a by-product of milling. It is used in skincare, especially K-beauty and J-beauty products, for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects .
Laboratory studies show that rice bran extracts contain antioxidants such as phenolic acids, anthocyanins (in pigmented rice), tocopherol and gamma-oryzanol , and that a fermented extract reduced melanin-related signaling in mouse melanoma cells . The sources reviewed contain no controlled human trial of topical rice bran extract for skin tone; the Grokipedia article describes clinical results, but it is AI-generated and its citations were not independently verified here.

name: Flutamide topical (melasma)

angle.text: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen, studied off-label as a 1% topical for melasma to even out facial pigmentation. The evidence base for that use is thin.

summary: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen studied as a 1% topical for melasma, with a thin evidence base and liver warnings on the oral drug.

currentQuick:
Flutamide is an antiandrogen pill used for prostate cancer. A 1% topical version has been tried for melasma as an alternative to hydroquinone.
Only a single randomized comparison with hydroquinone was found cited, without reported results.
How it works: It blocks androgen receptors. How this would affect melasma pigmentation is not explained in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: The oral drug is associated with severe liver injury and is prescription-only. Safety of the topical form was not documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen taken by mouth, used mainly for prostate cancer. It blocks androgen receptors . A 1% topical preparation has been studied as an alternative treatment for melasma, a pigmentation disorder of the face .
Wikipedia's melasma article cites a randomized trial that compared topical 1% flutamide with hydroquinone but does not report its results or safety profile . The oral drug carries a warning for severe liver injury ; the sources reviewed contain no data on systemic absorption or safety of the topical form.
